questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I just asked myself: where would I like to live for 4 months if I could chose anywhere. I then chose Montreal in Canada because I thought of Canada as a friendly country with a beautiful nature and a diverse culture. I chose Montreal specifically because of the French language. Furthermore, I wanted to have courses concerning politics in the North American continent - but without being in the US because of the political situation there.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Montreal is a very cool, vibrant city. Regarding Concordia University, I was happy about both the social and academic stuff. Concordia had a lot of exchange student events and the administration is generally helpful. Overall, a smooth experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There is a lot of info and deadlines no matter where you go. But I would say Concordia was good at sending reminder e-mails and e-mails that laid out the process. The International student center was not always super elaborate in their responses to my questions, but they answered very quickly, and when I needed help they set up a virtual meeting with me. I would say overall that the information was accessible, and Concordia was informative.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The International student center sends out weekly reminder e-mails about deadlines and what is happening for exchange students through out the whole semester which are nice. You also get a specific advisor from the international student center who you can contact.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The information was accessible and you receive a lot of e-mails about deadlines and so on. In general, concordia is helpful. I would say that my specific advisor replied fast but very limited to my questions and was not always a big help.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found housing on the KU-made "students going to Canada" group where another Danish student wrote out that she had a room, she was not going to use because she had multiple options. It was my first and only request for housing, so that was very easy. A lot of my friends also live in residences. The advantage of finding something on your own might be that you can find something not around downtown but in other areas such as Plateau for instance which is a super nice area that I have been so happy to live in!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Maybe it is a little more expensive, but that depends a lot. Again, the advantage might be to be able to choose to live somewhere else than around Downtown - I can highly recommend the Plateau area! I lived very smoothly with two Canadian girls. A nice thing about renting rooms here is that you often do not pay a deposit beforehand. You just pay the monthly rent.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I lived in an amazing area for 4.500 dkk which I think is a fair price considering the quality of the apartment (relatively big room, everything worked, also quite cozy older building) and the area. Montreal is still not as crazy expensive compared to many other North American cities.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall good, but it is never just easy going on exchange I think. Read the mails thoroughly, make a to do list and reach out and ask if you have questions. But also believe that it will work out, because it probably will! It seems more confusing that it actually is, and a lot of the "stress" is also just yourself stressing about wondering if you have everything under control. I was apparently late to the course registration, but I still got some nice courses, and they set up a virtual meeting with me immediately when they saw that I had not registered for the courses. I think Concordia and Canada are def not the worst places in terms of registration, information and structure.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
At Concordia, you have to apply already in the spring, if you are going in the spring semester (1 year before) instead of in the fall (half a year before) which most Canadian universities have as their deadline. This is important to know because it was not clear in the "introduction to exchange in Canada" presentation made by KU. This means that you should take the language test (duolingo is the cheapest), request temporary approval of courses and so on at this time. 
In the fall (I think november), you will receive an e-mail that it is time to chose courses. A specific deadline was not clear to me, but do it as quickly as possible, because the courses are taken quickly. Even though I was "late to the party" I still got some interesting courses after I talked with an advisor virtually. But I was also very open in terms of courses, so if you want some specific ones, be aware.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You are given a specific advisor - again mine was not of big help, but the person replied quickly and I could also reach out to the general international student office which also replied quickly and helped. Concordia in general sent a lot of e-mails including information about webinars which were good to attend.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was a little late register for courses, but Concordia was very helpful about it, and I still got some nice ones

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be aware of the earlier deadline than many other Canadians universities (if you are going in the spring semester, the deadline is in the spring semester before - 1 year before).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I got some nice courses - especially considering that many were taken when I registered

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The academic level is fine - somewhat like the level at home. The amount of assigned readings are basically the same. The difference is the work load throughout the semester. There are more smaller tests and in that way you have to be more up to date with your readings before the exam period compared to at home, but actually I found it nice because it also lowers the pressure on one single exam (the final exam counting approx 40% of your final grad). A big help is of course that the grades get transferred as passed/failed.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
There are more smaller tests throughout the semester, but also class activities like small quizzes on the assigned readings and stuff like that. You do not have to be fully prepared for every course though, but I read considerably more throughout the semester than at home. This also depends on your own expectations to yourself and what you want to get out of the courses as the courses get transferred as passed/failed.

A big difference is that these smaller tests throughout the semester are closed book, in-hand assignments mostly due to AI. This sounded a little scary to me but I have actually ended up enjoying it!

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
American Foreign policy (interesting course, one of the more hardcore courses, but not un-doable at all)
Race and ethnic relations (sociology/anthropology course, very interesting and a different way of teaching than classic political science courses)
Canadian politics (can highly recommend for exchange students - Canada is politically a very interesting country and you learn about its systems pros and cons compared to the American and British systems) 
Comparative democratization (almost exactly the same course as DAK3 at political science at KU. Maybe a little too much the same as a course I have already completed at home). 

In general, you can definitely feel you have some relevant background knowledge if you take BA courses as a MA student, but I will still say I learned a lot of new things/developed my former understanding of different concepts and theories. I am glad that I had a socio/anthro course as well to mix things up a bit.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: American foreign policy was really interesting - also to see it through Canadian eyes. Race and ethnic relations was very interesting - also to have this course in such a diverse country as Canada. Canadian politics gives you a good and relevant understanding of the country you are in, and if you think at first it sounds too niche, it is just as much about pros and cons of presidentialism, parliamentarism, federalism and other concepts.

questions.answer: Cafes/restaurants are basically the same as in Copenhagen or maybe a little cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were a lot of exchange students events and trips. The Concordia outdoor club is nice for hiking and outdoor activities.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of different ones and you well-informed of them via instagrams and mails.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The Concordia outdoor club and just attending the exchange student events. The quality of them may vary a bit but is it just an easy way to meet new people and then you can plan your own things to do together. I would not recommend joining the Home room initiative. Maybe I was just unlucky with my group, but I felt like the facilitation was not very good.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Going on hikes and in general get the best out of the cold and long Montreal winter. Concodia outdoor club offers different hikes, skip trip and snow tubing. The Montreal hiking community (mtlhiking on insta) i s also a good site to know. You can also visit Quebec city or Toronto - both nice cities. Montreal in itself has a lot to offer. A looot of good cafes/restaurant/bars and a lot of vintage shopping. Many also go to New York by bus e.g.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Montreal is a very international and diverse city, and even though it is in Quebec people speak English everywhere.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Because of the city's internationality and diversity, people are very open. I would say I spent most of my time with exchange students though.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None really

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The diversity and the mix between European culture and American culture

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- dont be scared of the French language. There are many English courses and everyone speaks English
- I did not talk a lot with people in my classes, and a great deal of my friends had the same experience. Even though Canadians are open, the culture seems to be more individualistic in terms of attending classes. You walk in, you attend and you leave again. For me it was just fine - you have so many other things going on. Focus on the exchange students I would say. 
- the downtown area around Concordia is cool, but also make your way to Plateau and mile end area. These areas are cool in another way and a great place to sit at nice cafes and do your studying.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I signed up for the Jumelage program which Concordia will inform you about in one of their mails after you have arrived. It is a program where you are being matched with someone who talks a language that you would like to get better, at and you in exchange teach the other person a language they would like to get better at. You get matched for free and then you have to design your weekly meetings and how you would like to do it yourselves. For me it was a good experience (I learned French and I taught the other person English). It is just as much a cultural experience as it is a language-learning experience.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I think living in Montreal was a very big reward in itself. I really like the "vibe" here. To get to know Canada as a country with all its nuances (colonial history, Indigenous history and how it copes with its complicated past) has also been interesting. Of course the people I met here have had a very big influence on my stay and I have made some very nice friendships.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I did not know anyone here before coming so that was of course something I was both excited but also nervous about. But it has been a really rewarding experience and something I think everyone should try!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
